title: Matter, breath and the two paths
hookLine: the first student asks where living things come from, and Pippalada answers with a pair: matter and breath, moon and sun
carry: the ancestors' path returns; the gods' path doesn't

lines: SIR, WHERE DO CREATURES COME FROM?
cards: The six students have kept the discipline. The first to step forward is Kabandhi Katyayana, with a question as old as asking: sir, from where are these creatures born? Children ask some version of it.
Where did I come from? Where did the dog come from, the ants, the trees? A biologist would answer one way, a grandmother another.
Pippalada answers with a story, and at its center is a pair, two things that need each other, the way a song needs both silence and sound.

teach.b: Pippalada says: Prajapati, the lord of creatures, wanted offspring.

teach.h: RAYI IS MATTER; PRANA IS BREATH.
teach.b: He did tapas, the inner heat you met with Bhrigu, and from that heat he produced a pair: rayi and prana. Rayi means wealth, substance, matter: the stuff that takes form. Prana is breath, life, the energy that moves it.
Then the pair shows up everywhere. The sun is prana. The moon is rayi.
Matter and life, always in pairs. Then the answer turns to people. The year itself is Prajapati, and it has two paths, a southern and a northern.

teach.h: GOOD WORKS: THE MOON, AND BACK.
teach.b: Those who honor sacrifice and good works, digging wells, giving, keeping the rites, take the southern path, the path of the ancestors, the pitryana, to the world of the moon. And from there they return, to be born again.

teach.h: TAPAS, FAITH, KNOWLEDGE: THE SUN, NO RETURN.
teach.b: Those who seek the self through tapas, a disciplined life, faith and knowledge take the northern path, to the sun, which later tradition calls the path of the gods.
That, the text says, is the resting place of breath, the immortal, the fearless. From there they do not return.
This is an early form of a teaching every Hindu grows up with: karma, the way how you live shapes the next birth, and moksha, freedom from the circle.
The Gita names the two paths too. So when a Hindu grandmother says feeding people is good for the next life, she's on the moon's path. And the hope underneath it is the sun's.

how: Many Hindus mark the sun's northward turn at Makar Sankranti in mid-January and treat the northern half of the year, uttarayana, as an auspicious time, an idea that echoes the two paths of texts like this one.

o: matter, the stuff that takes form
breath, the life that moves the body
the sun's path north, of no return

games.q: the pair in everything — tap the pairs.

s: it means wealth, substance, matter: the stuff that takes form.
in the text, those on the southern path return
the path of the ancestors leads to the world of the moon, and back.
sir, from where are these creatures born?

games.q: Nani hopes her pujas and feeding people bring her a good next life. her sister, who meditates every dawn, hopes not to come back at all. in the Prashna, which paths are these?
o: both the same path, the sun's.
Nani: the ancestors' path, to the moon and back; her sister: the northern path, to the sun, no return.
Nani: the sun's path; her sister: no path at all.
games.why: good works and rites lead by the southern path to the moon, and back to birth. tapas, faith and knowledge of the self lead north, to the sun, the fearless, from which there's no return.

practice: Feel the body's weight, the bones and muscle, the pressure where you touch the chair or floor: that's rayi, matter, the moon side. Then feel the breath moving through it, warming and lifting it: that's prana, the sun side.
Rest on both at once, the stillness that holds and the motion that lives; neither one is enough alone.

wordCard.voice: Rayi, wealth and matter, paired with prana, breath. Where do creatures come from? From rayi and prana, the moon and the sun, which Prajapati made as a pair.

orig.note: Sanskrit rayi: wealth, substance, matter. paired with prāṇa, breath, in Prashna 1.4.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: the ancestors' path returns; the gods' path doesn't. That's week fifty-eight: the person, hunger and thirst, the door at the top, three births, the great saying, six students, and matter and breath. Day four hundred six.
